summary: This memo describes the status of the development and deployment of CIDR, a way to manage IP address space that allows routes to be aggregated. It replaces RFC 1367, which was a deployment schedule. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This is a progress report on a change that helped the Internet's address book stay small and manageable. It is historic.

subtitle: A mid-1993 progress report on getting CIDR and BGP-4 into Internet routers before the routing tables grew too large.

tldr.problem: The Internet was growing exponentially. Handing out ever more network numbers strained the registries, router forwarding tables were getting large, and poor use of Class A and Class B addresses threatened to exhaust them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reports on the schedule of address-management steps from RFC 1367, which milestones were met, how far router vendors had got with BGP-4 support for CIDR, and how fast route counts were growing against router capacity.
tldr.outcome: All the milestones except the delivery and installation of CIDR software were met. The RFC is a snapshot of one moment, it replaces RFC 1367, and it is now Historic.

today: RFC 1467 is Historic. It replaced RFC 1367, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. It records the state of CIDR deployment in August 1993 and is not a specification.

sections.title: Why CIDR Was Needed
sections.content:
The Internet's exponential growth caused three problems named in the RFC. Allocating more and more IP network numbers wore on the organizations doing it. The number of reachable network numbers taxed the ability of some routers to manage their forwarding tables. And poor use of allocated network numbers threatened to deplete the Class A and Class B address space.

The community agreed on mid-term mechanisms, with more fundamental protocol changes being explored for the long term. US Federal Agencies proposed procedures to help deploy them, first in RFC 1366, later made obsolete by RFC 1466. A schedule for implementing the procedures came in RFC 1367 in October 1992.
sections.eli5: The Internet was handing out addresses faster than it could keep tidy lists of them, so people agreed on a plan to hand them out in neater groups.

sections.title: Milestones Met and Missed
sections.content:
Most milestones of the RFC 1367 schedule were met on time. From 31 October 1992, criteria for regional address registries were in place, and the RIPE NCC became a regional registry, given the block 194.0.0.0 to 195.255.255.255 to administer for Europe. Class A numbers were put on reserve, Class B numbers were issued only when reasonably justified, and a block of Class C numbers was issued instead of a Class B whenever possible. The schedule was re-evaluated on 14 February 1993 and left unchanged. From 15 April 1993 the Internet Registry allocated all networks in appropriately sized blocks of Class C numbers.

Network service providers also took blocks of Class C space to hand on to their clients, which began to move address registration to a more regional level. The RFC says this worked as hoped, with no major problems.

One milestone was not met. The schedule said an address aggregation mechanism would be generally available on 6 June 1993. That date slipped, though the RFC says continuing the schedule had not significantly added to the Internet's problems.
sections.eli5: Nearly every step on the checklist was ticked off on time. The one that was late was getting the new software into the routers.

sections.title: Router Vendors and BGP-4
sections.content:
The RFCs on address management do not depend on any specific aggregation technology, but the community agreed to use Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR). CIDR is supported by BGP-4 and IDRP, and most vendors were doing BGP-4 first, so BGP-4 would carry the initial deployment.

The RFC then reports each vendor's status in alphabetical order, with the caveat that some speculation is involved. 3Com had BGP-4 code tested internally that accepts, forwards and manages aggregated routes, but not yet code that forms aggregates. ANS had a BGP-4 implementation in internal testing. BBN planned to finish BGP-4 development by early Summer 1994. Cisco had pre-Beta code that implements aggregation. Proteon's initial code would support neither aggregation nor de-aggregation. Wellfleet aimed at beta code in roughly early 1994, including controlled de-aggregation.
sections.eli5: The new rule book for routers was written, but each router maker still had to teach its machines to read it. Some were nearly there and some were months away.

sections.title: Growth Rate and Router Capacity
sections.content:
MERIT's counts of networks in the NSFNET/ANSNET policy routing database showed growth of approximately 8% per month, a doubling every nine or ten months. The database held over 13K networks, though not all were active. The 10K active mark was passed in late June. The RFC projected that 12K active networks would be reached in about late September 1993 and 25K in mid-94, assuming the same rate.

Networks outside the NSFNET/ANSNET database added less than 25% on top. The RFC expected CIDR to have a significant impact on forwarding table size and its rate of growth, and noted that a study of the impact had been started at the July 1993 BGP Deployment Working Group meeting.

Providers' routers had limits. ALTERNET carried about 11K to 12K routes and could support up to about 35K, and the RFC expected processing capacity to run out before memory. All ANSNET routers ran AIX 3.2, which supports up to 12K networks, with a next version supporting 25K. EBONE carried about 10K to 11K routes and each new transatlantic link would increase BGP table memory by approximately 20%. ESNET's problem was storing configuration of which networks to accept, not table size. SPRINTLINK and ICM nodes carried about 11K to 12K routes and were expected to support up to about 25K.
sections.eli5: The Internet's list of networks was doubling about every nine or ten months, and the routers could only hold so many entries. Grouping addresses together was meant to stop the lists from overflowing.

viz.caption: SCHEDULE MILESTONES REPORTED IN THE RFC

events.label: 31 October: schedule of RFC 1367 starts; regional registries and Class A reserve
14 February: schedule re-evaluated and left unchanged
15 April: all networks allocated in blocks of Class C numbers
6 June: target for aggregation; this milestone slipped
